newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodian vote for new premier undemocratic - U.S.
newsitem.headline: Cambodian vote for new premier undemocratic - U.S.

text.p: The replacement of ousted Prince Norodom Ranariddh as first premier by Foreign Minister Ung Huot was not democratic given the atmosphere of intimidation in Cambodia, a U.S. Embassy official said on Thursday.

"While we respect Ung Huot as an individual, in the absence of a return by FUNCINPEC members of parliament in exile, and in the current atmosphere of intimidation, we do not believe yesterday's votes were democratic," an embassy spokesperson told Reuters.
"We hope that FUNCINPEC will revisit this issue when a genuinely free and open environment returns to Phnom Penh," the spokesperson said.

The National Assembly voted by secret ballot on Wednesday to accept Ung Huot's nomination as first prime minister. It also voted by a show of hands to strip Ranariddh of his parliamentary immunity, clearing the way for his prosecution for alleged crimes if he returns to Cambodia.

Many supporters of Ranariddh's FUNCINPEC party fled from the country in the wake of Hun Sen's bloody July 6 takeover and a subsequent crackdown on the party in which some 40 people were killed, according to United Nations human rights officials.
Among those who fled were some 20 members of parliament from FUNCINPEC and a small allied party. Ninety-nine of the assembly's 120 members were present for Wednesday's votes.
Ung Huot, who was chosen to replace Ranariddh by FUNCINPEC members who remained in the country, told reporters on Thursday he had yet to hear of the U.S. position and he declined to comment on it.

The U.S. embassy spokesperson said that after Wednesday's vote, Ung Huot told parliament he remained committed to the 1991 Paris Peace accords, which ended Cambodia's war and paved the way for U.N.-supervised elections in 1993, and he was also committed to holding another general election next year.
"We urge the Cambodian government to follow through on this commitment," the U.S. official said.
Members of the Cambodian opposition in Bangkok said on Wednesday that Ung Huot's nomination was illegal and in violation of the Cambodian constitution.
The constitution requires that a new first prime minister be approved by the king and both the president and the two vice presidents of the National Assembly.
One of the assembly's vice presidents, Son Soubert, has joined the opposition in exile and said he did not support Ung Huot's nomination.

King Norodom Sihanouk said late last month he would not recognise Ung Huot as first premier as the post belonged to his son. The king also said that a vote on a new first prime minister by an incomplete parliament would be invalid.
The United States and the Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) both said soon after the prince's ouster that they still recognised the prince as first prime minister.

Indonesia, whose foreign minister Ali Alatas heads a three-member mediation team on Cambodia, said on Wednesday that any ASEAN comment on Ung Huot's election would have to wait until a meeting in Singapore next week.

The prince was out of the country at the time of his ouster. Hun Sen said later Ranariddh was free to come back, but that he would have to face charges for his illegal negotiations with the outlawed Khmer Rouge guerrilla group and for alleged weapons smuggling.
The prince has dismissed the accusations and called from abroad for opposition to his former co-premier and coalition partner.
